items.title: China cancels ALL refined product exports ex-HK/Macau, effective immediately, no end date
items.idea: China is the only place on Earth with excess refining capacity. The ban lands while the global product market is already described as 'horrendous'. Flashback: China's crude-buying pause in March-July marked the start of the big crude drop.
items.angle: Products, not crude, are where the squeeze lives. Long cracks / diesel vs short front-month crude is the cleaner expression.
items.tweetA: The one swing exporter of refined product just switched off. Crude is the headline; the crack spread is the trade. $VLO $MPC $PSX
items.tweetB: March: China stops buying crude, crude falls. October: China stops selling product. Same lever, opposite sign. Who is long the other side of this?

items.title: China's product inventories are at decade lows - the buffer that existed in March is gone
items.idea: Refinery runs were throttled back since the Iran war began as crude imports fell, with no demand destruction. China doesn't disclose commercial or SPR stocks, so the decade-low read is inferred. China has 'exhausted most of the levers' it used early in the war.
items.angle: This is why the export ban is not a repeat of March. The domestic market no longer has slack to absorb it, so the ban is binding, not symbolic.
items.tweetA: In March Beijing could ban exports because the tanks were full. Now they're banning exports because the tanks are empty. Different motive, same headline, very different price impact.
items.tweetB: Everyone priced China as a demand story. It's a product-supply story. A country with no inventory cushion and the world's spare refining capacity just closed the door.

items.title: Diesel nightmare scenario: China ban + a US diesel export ban 'sends global diesel prices through the roof'
items.idea: Hfir flags the conditional: if the US announces a diesel export ban on top of China's, global diesel reprices violently. MacroEdge separately says a US export suspension is possible but an EU diesel release is the likelier compromise.
items.angle: Two oil desks, same event, different odds on the US move. Position for the tail via ULSD calls, not outright crude.
items.tweetA: Hfir: US diesel export ban = diesel through the roof. MacroEdge: threat is more powerful than the ban. Both can be right. The threat alone prices it. $HO $VLO
items.tweetB: A US export ban is the one move that makes the China ban look small. I'd want to know how many days of US distillate cover exist before the midterms. Nobody publishes that number.

items.title: Export ban timing + new Iranian attacks on the Oman lane = 'no deal reached with the US'
items.idea: Hfir reads the timing of China's ban, coupled with additional Iranian attacks on the Oman lane, as a signal that talks with the US failed. Muscat as the venue/route is the pressure point.
items.angle: Market was pricing a deal. If the read is right, front-end crude is mispriced and risk premium returns via products first.
items.tweetA: China shuts product exports the same day Iran hits the Oman lane. Coincidence is a hard sell. If the deal is dead, what's in the price?
items.tweetB: Hormuz flows 'oscillating higher', Oman lane under fire, China pulling product off the market. Three signals pointing the same way and crude is still waiting for a headline.

items.title: Diesel printed an all-time high this morning; Dec-2027 crude at a cycle high
items.idea: ULSD/gasoil and RBOB look more constructive than CL. The back of the curve (CLZ27) hit a cycle high while the front end stays calm - MacroEdge reads this as 'patience through October' being priced into the deferred contracts.
items.angle: Curve steepening at the back plus ATH diesel is a regime signal, not a spike. Watch product-vs-crude spread versus equities.
items.tweetA: Diesel at an all-time high, Dec-27 crude at a cycle high, front-month crude calm. The market is telling you the problem is long-dated and in the barrel you can't crack.
items.tweetB: Everyone's staring at the WTI front month. The ATH is in diesel. If you only own crude exposure, you own the wrong end of this.

charts.desc: CLZ2027 chart plus pennant retest chart, per text

items.title: Final SPR loan: draws return to 3-6mb/week through mid-December
items.idea: The latest SPR loan is the last of the war allocation from March on. After a slow drip of hundreds of thousands b/d, draws go back to 3-6 million barrels/week for ~8 weeks, running to mid-Dec - i.e. past the midterms. Sustainable Hormuz flow estimated ~70% of pre-war.
items.angle: Policy put on WTI through the election. Squeeze-driven upside is the path; fundamentals pull the other way.
items.tweetA: SPR at 3-6mb/week to mid-December is the most expensive election-year price control in history. You can cap WTI. You can't cap diesel with crude barrels.
items.tweetB: 70% of pre-war Hormuz flow as the 'new normal' means the market has quietly accepted a permanent 30% haircut. Then SPR is bridge financing for an outage with no end date.

items.title: US gasoline inventories lowest since 2014 with ~6 weeks of draws left - priced in products, not CL
items.idea: MacroEdge says the tightness is being priced 'more accurately in refined product pricing rather than the front-month', which 'makes very little sense relative to everything else'. Also flags a chart on Venezuela imports.
items.angle: Spread trade: product crack vs flat price. Also relevant to the Venezuela barrel debate.
items.tweetA: Gasoline stocks at the lowest since 2014. Six weeks of draws left. Front-month crude barely cares. One of these two markets is wrong and I know which one has the physical.
items.tweetB: The Venezuela import chart is the quiet story here. If US refiners are leaning on Venezuelan heavy to keep runs up, the barrel is a geopolitical position, not just an oil one.

charts.desc: Venezuela imports chart (per text) + CL pennant retest

items.title: Iran has a ~2 week window to escalate before the midterms; WTI $95+ is the trigger level
items.idea: If Iran wants WTI back at $95+, which recently drove product pricing hard, it must move in the next two weeks. MacroEdge calls escalation a coin toss; 'economic war' remains the focus. The Administration will pull every lever to hold WTI down until the election. Support base now $80-82.
items.angle: A dated catalyst and a defined level. Good for vol structure, not direction.
items.tweetA: Iran's escalation window is about two weeks. The US administration's price-control window is about five. Someone's clock runs out first. $CL $USO
items.tweetB: Midterm oil politics is a game with a deadline on both sides. The unusual part: only one side's lever (SPR) is public.

items.title: US10Y has broken through 5%; bond vol 'exploded' - and it's real yields doing it
items.idea: Move is driven by real yields with no meaningful participation from inflation expectations. Causes: crisis-level procyclical deficits worldwide, Iran war supply shocks, AI/military buildout demand shocks, hiking central banks, hyperscaler competition for capital. US debt breached $40T.
items.angle: Term premium regime. Own the curve view, not the Fed view.
items.tweetA: 10Y through 5% on real yields, breakevens asleep. That isn't an inflation scare, it's a clearing-price problem: $40T of debt plus hyperscalers all bidding for the same capital.
items.tweetB: Hyperscaler capex is competing with the Treasury for savings. When both fund at 5%+, one of them has to blink first. My money's not on the one with the printing press.

items.title: Core PCE came in well under consensus - rates rallied, then sold off to new cyclical highs
items.idea: A benign inflation print couldn't hold a bid in bonds. Context from the note: Q2 GDP revised to 2.2%, Atlanta Fed GDPNow ~5% for Q3. Bonds 'brushed it off as noise'.
items.angle: When good news gets sold, the market is trading supply, not data.
items.tweetA: Soft core PCE and Treasuries made new lows anyway. That's the market telling you the data isn't the driver. Supply is.
items.tweetB: GDPNow at 5% for Q3 with a PCE miss. Goldilocks, except the bond market refuses to play along.

items.title: Equal-weight SPX trending straight down while cap-weight sits a hair off ATH; CCC- spreads widened substantially
items.idea: Real yields up, inflation expectations flat, FCIs loose: the 'everything is fine' story holds in upper tranches of credit and equity indices only. Beneath: equal-weight S&P falling and CCC- spreads wide.
items.angle: Dispersion trade: the index lies, the tail credit tells the truth.
items.tweetA: SPX a hair off the high. RSP in a straight line down. CCC- spreads blowing out. Pick the one you trust.
items.tweetB: Financial conditions indices are loose because they're cap-weighted. The weakest credits are already in a tighter regime than the index admits.

items.title: 'Bonds are starting to look attractive for the first time in years' - and Don calls Fed obsession a joke until fiscal moves
items.idea: Allocators who fled to PE, private credit and hedge funds due to low yields now have a convex, growth-hedging option. Separately Don argues nobody in politics is talking about spending cuts, bond vigilantes are 'comfortable turning up the heat' and bond longs have bled since the Iran war began; stripping energy from inflation is 'embarrassing' because petroleum is in every supply chain.
items.angle: Flow regime shift: long bonds as the late-cycle hedge again.
items.tweetA: After a decade of buying illiquid alts to escape 2% yields, allocators get a 5% duration option with real convexity. The marginal buyer is about to rotate and nobody has modeled where from.
items.tweetB: Core inflation 'ex-energy' is a metric for a world where energy isn't in the supply chain. That world doesn't exist. Petroleum is in everything. Fed models that strip it are fitting noise.

items.title: 'There Is No Free Boom': fiscal, not the Fed, is driving the cycle (Shah)
items.idea: Input-cost inflation is at its highest since October 2022 as demand meets supply constraints and higher energy costs. Shah's framework: strong demand, loose fiscal, AI investment boom and a less globalised world mean inflation pressure can persist long after the first shock. Monetary policy is 'no longer the main character'.
items.angle: Fiscal dominance is the thesis. It explains why cuts don't move 10s.
items.tweetA: Input cost inflation is at the highest since Oct 2022. Fed has 'caught up with the economy' - and it doesn't matter, because Treasury is driving.
items.tweetB: Boom plus deglobalization plus AI capex plus deficits. Every one of those is a structural, not cyclical, source of inflation. Cutting rates into that is the cleanest bet on being wrong.

items.title: Falling token prices don't mean falling compute demand; frontier capability is running well ahead of enterprise adoption (Shah)
items.idea: Diffusion could keep inference demand growing for years: cheaper intelligence unlocks far more workflows and agents. The gap between what models can do and what firms have deployed is the runway.
items.angle: Jevons for tokens. Bullish compute, bearish anyone modelling capex off per-token revenue.
items.tweetA: Token prices falling 10x is not a demand problem, it's a unit economics unlock. Every cost curve in history that fell this fast created more consumption, not less. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: Capability is ahead of adoption by quarters, maybe years. That's an inventory of deployable demand nobody has booked yet.

items.title: The AI race may be decided by diffusion: China's edge in factories, robots, power and deployment (Shah)
items.idea: 'The big question is no longer who builds the smartest model first, but who can actually diffuse that intelligence across the economy fastest.' US may keep the model lead; China's strengths are hardware, power and deployment infrastructure.
items.angle: Pairs with the onchain robotics piece. Shenzhen supply chain vs frontier labs.
items.tweetA: The US is optimizing for the best model. China is optimizing for the most robots running it. Only one of those shows up in GDP.
items.tweetB: Model lead has a half-life of months. A factory base has a half-life of decades. Which one are you long?

items.title: Krinsky (BTIG): S&P flat, median stock down sharply, semis doing the heavy lifting
items.idea: The index hides a much weaker market underneath. Breakouts are failing, follow-through is poor, investors are punished for chasing strength while downside moves stick. Goldman adds that investors are still adding exposure without conviction.
items.angle: Narrow leadership plus a hedging bid. Frame: how much of the index is one sector.
items.tweetA: S&P unchanged, median stock down hard, semis carrying the tape. That's not a bull market, that's a single-sector rally with an index wrapper.
items.tweetB: Adding exposure without conviction is the setup for air pockets. Buyers with no thesis are the first sellers.

items.title: Treasury vol surging, HY CDX wider, equity vol contained - 'rarely stays unresolved'
items.idea: Rates and credit flash warning lights while equity vol stays low. Oil can fall while yields keep climbing, so the bond problem is becoming structural, not geopolitical.
items.angle: Vol cross-asset: equity vol is the cheapest hedge of the three.
items.tweetA: MOVE up, HY CDX wider, VIX calm. Equity vol is the only one of the three not pricing the same risk. Guess which gets repriced.
items.tweetB: Crude falls, yields rise. The oil-to-rates link broke. That means the bond selloff has a different cause and a longer shelf life.

items.title: Micron guides next-quarter revenue midpoint $61.5B, ~7% above the Street; EPS $38.15
items.idea: Beat and raise: revenue and non-GAAP EPS ahead, guidance well above consensus. Goldman raised target to $1,250.
items.angle: Memory is the second leg of the AI trade. Pair with semis carrying the index.
items.tweetA: $61.5B guide, 7% above the Street, for a memory company. Ten years ago this was a commodity cycle chart. $MU
items.tweetB: Goldman's $1,250 target on Micron. Where was this stock in 2022? Memory just got repriced from commodity to AI infrastructure.

items.title: Micron margin guide 86.3% vs 87.4% consensus: higher-cost inventory plus comp expense
items.idea: The one soft spot in the quarter: Goldman attributes the near-term drag to higher-cost inventory moving through and increased compensation expense. Part of the pressure should ease the following quarter.
items.angle: A margin miss in a beat-and-raise, the kind of detail that decides next-day price action.
items.tweetA: 86.3% vs 87.4%: a margin miss on a guide this big. When the bear case is 'comp expense', it tells you how strong the quarter was. $MU
items.tweetB: A memory maker arguing about gross margin in the 80s. That is not a commodity business anymore. Please revisit your comps.

items.title: Micron: 5-year customer agreements cover ~35% of expected revenue through FY30; $55B FY27 capex
items.idea: About three-quarters of the agreements have structured pricing. Capacity added with $55B FY27 capex is years away, supply remains tight through 2028. Goldman's own model shows growth slowing after 2027 and margins easing into 2029.
items.angle: Memory becoming contract-based is the cycle-breaker. Also shows Goldman is modelling the peak already.
items.tweetA: Long-term contracts on 35% of revenue to FY30. That's a cyclical business writing itself a floor. The market hasn't priced a memory company that can't have a bust. $MU $SNDK
items.tweetB: $55B of FY27 capex with supply still tight through 2028. Goldman has growth slowing after 2027. The peak is in the sell-side model before it's in the price.

items.title: ASML: €591B, +88% in a year; EUV machine costs ~$400M, 100,000+ parts, 200 principal suppliers
items.idea: FT profile: the machine is the size of a double-decker bus, fires 60,000 molten-tin droplets per second, each blasted by a laser into plasma emitting 13.5nm light. 2,000 companies in the supply chain. 'If a few billion dollars could buy another 20% of capacity, he would do it.' It can't.
items.angle: Capacity is physics-gated. ASML is the AI chokepoint beneath power, memory and packaging.
items.tweetA: 60,000 tin droplets a second. 100,000 parts. 2,000 suppliers. One company. You cannot capex your way out of that in a quarter. $ASML
items.tweetB: Europe's most valuable company is the only European one at the heart of AI, and it got there through patient engineering, not regulation. Compare to the AI Act debate.

items.title: TSMC as the 'Fed of AI', ASML as its printing press - and ASML is raising prices into TSMC resistance
items.idea: TSMC sets the supply of advanced chips by how much capacity it builds, like a central bank sets money supply. Every expansion is an ASML order. Demand is running ahead of supply for the rest of the decade, and ASML has been raising prices anyway.
items.angle: Pricing power at the very bottom of the stack.
items.tweetA: If TSMC is the Fed, ASML is the Bureau of Engraving. And the Bureau is raising its price per sheet. $TSM $ASML
items.tweetB: A supplier raising prices against its biggest customer's objections is the cleanest evidence of who holds the leverage in this stack.

items.title: ASML CEO: 'If you over-restrict, you bring desperation' - China >30% of Q2 shipments, Huawei building DUV
items.idea: US banned EUV exports to China but is far less strict on Nvidia selling EUV-made chips there. China remains a big DUV customer (over 30% of system shipments in Q2) while Huawei emerged as pivotal in domestic DUV. WSJ: without latest lithography, China could trail by 6-8 years by 2031.
items.angle: Export controls produce the competitor they aim to prevent. Asymmetry between chip sales and tool sales.
items.tweetA: ASML can't sell China its best machines. Nvidia can sell China chips made by them. One of those policies has a rationale, and it isn't the same one.
items.tweetB: 30% of shipments still go to China while Huawei builds the replacement. The customer is the competitor-in-training. Revenue today, a market share problem in 2031. $ASML

items.title: High-NA EUV: TSMC commits for 2030, Samsung deploys by 2028 for memory, Intel already taking delivery
items.idea: High-NA costs ~$400M each. Fouquet expects EUV to keep evolving for another 10-15 years, with transistors stacked on top of each other. ASML cracked EUV where Nikon and Canon couldn't via 'extreme co-operation': Zeiss optics, Trumpf lasers, VDL mechatronics, plus its 2012 sale of 23% to Intel/Samsung/TSMC and 2013 Cymer purchase. Also an 11% stake in Mistral AI.
items.angle: Memory-first High-NA at Samsung is the quiet link to the Micron news.
items.tweetA: Samsung puts High-NA into memory by 2028. TSMC waits until 2030. The memory makers are leading the logic foundry on the newest litho. That's new. $MU
items.tweetB: In 2012 ASML sold 23% of itself to its three biggest customers to fund EUV. Customers as investors. That's the real moat: a financing structure no competitor can copy.

items.title: 10y above 5.25%, yet BTC holds the mid-to-low $80ks - onchain behaviour looks like 'early innings' of a bull
items.idea: The main character is sovereign borrowing costs. All else equal that should weigh on BTC. Instead onchain investor behaviour is undergoing a classic reversal. Paywalled report; the note frames key regimes and tools for the cycle.
items.angle: BTC decoupled from rates is a relative strength signal.
items.tweetA: 10y over 5.25% and Bitcoin is sitting in the $80ks. In every prior regime that combination broke risk assets. This time it isn't. $BTC
items.tweetB: Rates up, BTC flat. Either crypto is decoupling or it's about to catch down. The onchain data says decoupling.

items.title: MSTR vs ASST: one treasury company is defensive, the other aggressive
items.idea: Checkonchain's comparative study of Strategy (MSTR) and Strive (ASST): 'One has adopted a more defensive stance, whilst the other is taking a more aggressive approach.' Details are paywalled.
items.angle: Bitcoin treasury-company strategy divergence under a higher-rate regime.
items.tweetA: Two BTC treasury companies, opposite playbooks, same 5% 10Y. One is hedging against the rate regime, one is leveraging into it. Only one of them survives a down year. $MSTR
items.tweetB: Cost of capital for BTC treasuries is the variable nobody models. At 5% the aggressive one needs BTC to compound above that just to stand still.

items.title: Onchain robotics: robotics a $7-9T market by 2050; hardware is 70%+ and China leads
items.idea: Parts can be sourced in Shenzhen/Shanghai and a robot assembled in days. The US can't compete on supply chain, so it competes on software/foundation models - the brains. Onchain robotics follows the same stance: funding teams without VC access and giving them tools.
items.angle: Crypto narrative with a real thesis: DePIN supplies data/infrastructure, not hardware.
items.tweetA: Robotics is 70% hardware and China owns the hardware. So the crypto robotics thesis is basically 'be the Anthropic to China's Foxconn'. It's a coherent idea. It's also a very early one.
items.tweetB: Every robotics map I see is drawn by the people who sell the tokens. The question is who pays for the data, and the answer is the same companies that don't need a token.

items.title: DePIN is the origin of onchain robotics: Geodnet sells centimeter-level GNSS data, buys back tokens
items.idea: Google Maps isn't accurate enough for self-driving cars, drones and mobile robots, which need centimeter accuracy. Geodnet sells satellite antennae to individuals on rooftops, forming a global navigation network. Miners get token rewards; Geodnet sells geospatial data to drone/robotics companies and most revenue goes to buybacks.
items.angle: Revenue-backed DePIN with a real buyer. The template to look for.
items.tweetA: Geodnet: people put antennae on their roofs, robotics firms buy the data, the revenue buys back the token. It's the rare DePIN with an actual customer.
items.tweetB: Centimeter-level positioning is a prerequisite for every autonomous system. The infrastructure layer is boring, essential and tokenizable. That's the opposite of most crypto.

items.title: AI risk goes mainstream: Americans now worry more about losing control of AI than about jobs
items.idea: Per Echelon polling, the top concern shifted from AI taking jobs earlier this year to AI getting too powerful to control. Trump and Harris voters are about equally concerned, and more Republicans want to slow AI than want to speed it. Bioterror risk worries Americans too.
items.angle: Regulatory-risk input: the political coalition for AI slowdown is bipartisan.
items.tweetA: The public fear flipped from 'AI takes my job' to 'AI escapes control'. And it's bipartisan. Betting on a permanent light-touch regime is a bet against the polling. $NVDA $MSFT
items.tweetB: Trump is the accelerationist and more Republicans want to slow AI than not. That's what a policy reversal looks like before it happens.

charts.desc: Echelon polls: concern flipping from jobs to loss of control; partisan split on slowing AI

items.title: 'Pacing the frontier': Fudenberg & Koh game-theory model of when AI leaders voluntarily slow down
items.idea: A leader comfortably ahead can slow for safety; with no clear leader, labs need transparency to slow together. Cited real-world echoes: Anthropic withholding Mythos and OpenAI pausing top-model development after some hacked the government. Noah's caveat: the model only works if safety research actually advances.
items.angle: Frame for lab strategy and for whether compute buildouts overshoot.
items.tweetA: Game theory says the leader can afford to slow down and the follower can't. Notice that every frontier lab claims to be the follower.
items.tweetB: If safety research isn't actually advancing, 'pacing the frontier' just means pausing to fill time. Who audits that?

items.title: Reindustrialization means processing minerals: China doesn't mine most critical minerals, it refines them
items.idea: Alexander Campbell's bottleneck charts show the roles roughly reversed since WW2. Other countries dig ore and ship it to China, which does the dirty, capital-intensive, low-margin chemical processing. US efforts: partnerships, industrial policy, even scrap-metal conservation.
items.angle: Processing capacity, not mine supply, is the investable gap.
items.tweetA: China's moat isn't the ore. It's the refining nobody else wanted to do because it was dirty and low-margin. That's a policy problem, not a geology one. $MP
items.tweetB: Rare earths get the headlines. The refining of copper, cobalt, lithium and gallium is the quieter version of the same chokepoint.

charts.desc: Campbell bottleneck charts: roles reversed since WW2; electric-tech mineral processing share

items.title: Rent is back to its pre-pandemic trend - and falling relative to wages. Supply worked.
items.idea: Apartment List shows rent stabilised and fell back to trend since 2022. Rent vs average hourly earnings of production workers: 2010s crisis real, 2022-23 pain lagged by lease rollovers, now more affordable than the late 2010s. Most apartments built since the 1980s; cities with the most supply saw the biggest rent declines.
items.angle: Shelter is the stickiest CPI component; supply is pulling it down.
items.tweetA: Rent is falling relative to wages in the cities that built the most. We ran the experiment and supply won. Shelter CPI is about to be the disinflation nobody credits. $XHB
items.tweetB: The inflation story keeps blaming oil, but the biggest CPI weight is quietly deflating because we poured concrete. That matters more than any Fed meeting.

charts.desc: Rent vs hourly earnings; apartment completions highest since the 1980s; city-level rent change vs supply

items.title: AI-exposed jobs have seen faster wage growth (Indeed); recent grads' unemployment did NOT spike in summer 2026 (Fairlie & Wu)
items.idea: Indeed: workers in AI-exposed jobs saw wages rise faster than less-exposed ones. Fairlie & Wu: using CPS microdata for Jun-Aug 2026, no spike in recent-grad unemployment relative to prior summers, older grads or non-grads. Adding 'wanting a job' adds ~2pp but still no significant rise.
items.angle: Counter to the 'entry-level apocalypse' narrative.
items.tweetA: AI exposure so far means higher pay, not unemployment. Recent grads' jobless rate didn't spike in summer 2026. The apocalypse trade has been early for two years.
items.tweetB: Exposure plus demand means wages. The worry should be less 'will AI replace me' and more 'is my job in the part of the economy AI is building out'.

charts.desc: Indeed AI-exposure wage chart; recent-grad unemployment chart

items.title: Digital media jobs are getting 'absolutely clobbered' by AI; live performing arts jobs held up
items.idea: Translator, trucker and radiologist jobs have all held up. Digital media is the first clear displacement category. Noah notes it matters because creative-plus-paid jobs are a dream for many.
items.angle: First clear occupation-level AI displacement signal in data.
items.tweetA: Radiologists fine. Truckers fine. Translators fine. Digital media jobs: collapsing. The first real displacement is in the occupation we told kids to pick.
items.tweetB: Live performance holds, digital doesn't. The line isn't skill, it's whether the product can be copied for free.

charts.desc: Occupation employment chart: digital media down vs live performing arts

items.title: Mass deportation isn't helping native-born workers (Konczal): unemployment higher, prime-age EPOP lower
items.idea: Native-born unemployment is higher than in Biden's last year and prime-age employment rates are lower. Native workers do worse where deportations are higher. Noah's logic: immigrants add labor demand as well as supply.
items.angle: Labor-supply shock thesis vs data; relevant for wage inflation reads.
items.tweetA: Deportations were sold as a jobs program for native workers. Native unemployment is higher, and worse where deportations are higher. Immigrants are also customers.
items.tweetB: If labor supply falls and employment falls with it, you have a demand shock, not a tightness story. Careful reading the next jobs report.

charts.desc: Konczal charts: native unemployment, EPOP, deportation intensity by region

items.title: China's loan growth has slowed to 4.9% - roughly nominal GDP - and manufacturing investment is falling
items.idea: Noah: 'bank loans are manufacturing' - factories full of robot arms were financed by loans. Banks are in balance-sheet repair mode despite government instructions. Rhodium's Logan Wright says the financial system is now what constrains growth, with a Japan-1990s trajectory of zombie firms.
items.angle: China credit impulse as the leading indicator for commodities and industrial exports.
items.tweetA: China loan growth is 4.9%, which is also about its GDP growth. The credit impulse has been zero for a while. Every 'China stimulus' trade assumes banks lend. They aren't. $FXI $KWEB
items.tweetB: Wright's point: the state controls the banks but not the lending decision. That's the Japan comparison I kept resisting. It's getting hard to.

charts.desc: China loan growth chart: decelerating to 4.9%

items.title: Why Noah isn't worried about AI cyber risk: in the long run, defense wins
items.idea: Any software can in principle be made impregnable if every vulnerability is removed, so as AI gets better at reading and rewriting code, defense eventually wins. Transition risk remains as AI-written code proliferates. The Hugging Face attack was the notable incident; no 'cyber 9/11' yet.
items.angle: Counter-view to AI-cyber fear trade; bio is the bigger tail.
items.tweetA: If AI can find every bug, it can also fix every bug. The scary period is the transition where attackers have it and defenders haven't deployed it. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: Noah is more worried about bio than code. Biology has no patch cycle. That asymmetry is the reason cyber stocks have a floor and biosecurity doesn't have a ticker.
